unbounded_read_on_the_failure_path.root_cause: `_tail()` called `read_text()` and took the last characters. Output was bounded; the read was not. The two are different guarantees and only one of them had been implemented.
unbounded_read_on_the_failure_path.reproduction: a multi-megabyte log read through a counting `io.open` wrapper recorded bytes far above the declared window while the returned string stayed small.
unbounded_read_on_the_failure_path.fix: one shared reader, `_bounded_tail`, seeks to `size - LOG_TAIL_BYTES` on the handle it is about to read and asks for `LOG_TAIL_BYTES + 1` bytes, so no call can read more than the window plus the probe byte; the size comes from that same handle, so a concurrent append cannot make the recorded size disagree with the read.

a_diagnostic_error_could_replace_the_lif.symptom: a `PermissionError`, an `OSError`, or a log deleted between the listing and the read escaped the sampler, so the published failure became the diagnostic's own stack rather than the uninstall refusal it was meant to describe.
a_diagnostic_error_could_replace_the_lif.root_cause: `log_state()` classified only `exists`, size and tail, and let any read exception propagate; the sampler as a whole had no containment either.
a_diagnostic_error_could_replace_the_lif.reproduction: opening a log whose read raises, or removing the file between the check and the read, produced an exception out of a function whose whole job was to add context.
a_diagnostic_error_could_replace_the_lif.fix: presence, measurability, readability and the read are four separate published facts; every `OSError` is classified by exception name with the `errno`/`winerror` copied off the object and no exception text transcribed; and a defect anywhere inside the sampler is published as `state="sampler_failed"` with `diagnostics unavailable (...)` while the lifecycle conclusion keeps being computed from the filesystem evidence.

reads_were_not_bounded_to_the_evidence_r.symptom: the digest of a path outside the isolated work root was refused, but the log reads themselves were not, and the install-tree count and its first names came from two separate listings that a concurrent delete could disagree about.
reads_were_not_bounded_to_the_evidence_r.root_cause: containment had been implemented where a defect had been visible (hashing) rather than wherever content could be published; the entry sample was assembled from two calls to `snapshot()`, which reports an empty mapping both for a missing directory and for an emptied one.
reads_were_not_bounded_to_the_evidence_r.reproduction: a log name inside the root whose resolved target lies outside it - on a POSIX host a symlink, on Windows the reparse point or junction recorded as such - was read and its content published; a snapshot double returning a different mapping per call produced a count that disagreed with the names beside it.
reads_were_not_bounded_to_the_evidence_r.fix: `permitted_root=work_root` on every lifecycle log read and on the uninstaller digest, refusing the read and publishing `skipped_unsafe_path` with `bytes_read=0`, and one `sorted(snapshot(...))` per sample feeding both the count and the names. platform_dependent_classification_caught.symptom: the first published run of this code failed both mandatory gates: on the Windows runner `tests\test_windows_release_evidence.py` reported `assert 'PermissionEr...inerror=None)' == 'not a regular file'`, and a sibling test disagreed about a byte count (24 against 23).
platform_dependent_classification_caught.root_cause: two Linux-flavoured assumptions. The module classified a directory through `IsADirectoryError`, which POSIX raises and Windows does not - the runner answered `PermissionError(errno=13)` for the same open - so the published reason depended on the platform while the fact did not. platform_dependent_classification_caught.reproduction: immediately available from the run's own annotations (a green local run was not enough, which is the point of publishing the failure rather than quietly re-running); and reproducible on any host from now on, because the new test makes `io.open` raise the Windows exception for a directory and asserts the platform-free classification.
platform_dependent_classification_caught.fix: the classification keys off `os.path.isdir` - the fact - so a directory reads "not a regular file" on every platform, with the state left at `unreadable`; the test compares the recorded size against the size the handle measured instead of a literal; and the checkpoint-shape guard that also failed on that run is satisfied by landing the record in the same commit as the guard, which had been the ordering mistake in the first place.
platform_dependent_classification_caught.not_relaxed: no expectation was weakened to obtain green: the failing assertions were replaced by equivalents that hold on both platforms (the size invariant is unchanged in meaning), one test was added, and the mutation battery grew a 27th entry that removes the new branch and is caught by it.

bounded_read_contract.limit: LOG_TAIL_BYTES = 512 * 1024 bytes (524288), documented at the constant and enforced by the seek window, not by the length of the returned string. A non-positive caller-supplied `byte_limit` raises ValueError: a programming error is not disguised as an environment condition.
bounded_read_contract.measured_not_asserted: `bytes_read` is the number of bytes the read returned and is published in every sample next to `read_state`, so the bound is auditable from the record; the shared test fixture counts bytes through a wrapped `io.open` in three independent cases (large log, one-line log, mid-character window), and a contract guard fails if any of those three measurements is deleted.
bounded_read_contract.decode_policy: UTF-8 with errors="replace"; a window that starts mid-character produces one U+FFFD, never a raised UnicodeDecodeError during a failure report. bounded_read_contract.states: complete, truncated, empty, absent, unreadable, skipped_unsafe_path - five of them are failures to read, and each says which; `truncated` is never described as the log.
bounded_read_contract.elision_marker: a clipped read announces itself inside the published text: "only the last N of M bytes were read; older content was not inspected", carried by the reason field and by _tail()'s bracketed prefix.
bounded_read_contract.publication_bound: independent of the read bound: each sampled tail is collapsed to one line and clipped again to 400 characters, so 512 KiB of tail never enters a step detail; widening that clip is caught by tests rather than by a comment.
bounded_read_contract.contents_stay_in_the_existing_channel: log content appears only under diagnostics.uninstall_forensics and the existing bounded, redacted diagnostic fields; no new published file, no environment dump, and no credential in an error or marker string because exception text is not transcribed.

race_safety.distinct_facts: exists, size_bytes, read_state, bytes_read and read_reason are recorded separately, so a log that is absent, one that is unreadable and one deliberately not read cannot be confused.
race_safety.never_raises: FileNotFoundError becomes `absent`; IsADirectoryError becomes "not a regular file"; any other OSError becomes `unreadable` with the class and codes; the launch error remains the finding.
race_safety.codes_are_copied: errno and winerror are read off the exception object, and a path that vanishes mid-check keeps the original error rather than replacing it with the sampler's.
race_safety.growth: the window is measured from the end and the read asks for one byte more, so a log that grows under the read is reported as truncated against the size it was measured at, without crashing.
race_safety.no_promotion: absent or unreadable evidence is never a pass: `uninstall_forensics` can only add context to a conclusion already computed from the install-tree checks, and a sampler failure leaves the verdict exactly where it was.

handle_anchored_confinement.permitted_root_anchor: the root is opened with O_RDONLY|O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW and every component is opened relative to that descriptor (`dir_fd`), so containment is structural rather than asserted; the final component adds O_NONBLOCK
handle_anchored_confinement.opened_object_validated: fstat on the opened descriptor; S_ISREG or nothing is read, which refuses a directory, a FIFO and a device with the same platform-free 'not a regular file' classification the gate learned to need in M42.8
handle_anchored_confinement.windows_method: no descriptor-relative open exists on Windows and the CRT O_NOFOLLOW is not a guard against junctions, so the verdict is bound to the handle: GetFileType must report a disk file, GetFileInformationByHandle supplies the volume serial, file index, size and attribute bits, and GetFinalPathNameByHandleW must lie under the root's own final path on the root's volume and be the object that was named -- a reparse attribute bit is refused on its own, and so is any handle whose metadata cannot be read
handle_anchored_confinement.root_identity_lifetime: `run_lifecycle` records the work root's identity once, when the run takes the directory, and every anchored open compares the object it reached against that record for the remainder of the run; a mismatch stops the reads with 'the directory behind the permitted root name is not the one this run created' rather than moving the boundary underneath them
handle_anchored_confinement.fail_closed: unavailable APIs, unreadable metadata, an unopenable root and an unclassifiable object all produce a bounded refusal state and zero bytes read; there is no fallback to a name-based open, and a refusal never becomes a lifecycle pass
handle_anchored_confinement.reads_covered: the four lifecycle log tails, the smoke log, the install-tree uninstaller digest, and the user-data sentinel content read; the installer's own digest is deliberately left name-based because its security check is the comparison against the published manifest SHA-256, which a substitution can only fail, and the artifact lives outside any root this step owns

platform_limits_stated_verbatim.windows_residual: CreateFileW resolves a link before a handle exists, so Windows is use-then-verify on the verified handle rather than an atomic open-by-descriptor; and a create on an object type that blocks would block before it can be classified. No ordinary file or directory can produce that block -- pipes live under \\.\pipe\, not inside a work root -- but a hostile mount point could, and on such a host the anchored open narrows the race rather than closing it.
platform_limits_stated_verbatim.both_platforms: what is closed on both platforms is the window between a name-based look and the open, for the shape that matters: a re-pointed name can no longer send content anywhere. What is *not* claimed is that an actor able to rename whole directories inside the private work root cannot substitute a different file that is also inside that root; the confinement rule protects the boundary, and a same-root substitution stays inside it.
platform_limits_stated_verbatim.simulated_is_not_native: the junction and reparse behaviour of the pure verdict function is tested on every host with fake handle metadata; the native junction test runs only where os.symlink can create one, is skipped on this Linux host, and is never counted as Windows coverage

tail_bound_ceiling.policy: LOG_TAIL_BYTES = 512 * 1024 is now a ceiling rather than a default: `byte_limit` may be lower, and a higher value raises ValueError before any file is opened; MAX_TAIL_READ_BYTES = 524289 is the most any single read may fetch
tail_bound_ceiling.why_not_clamped: a clamp would report a smaller read than the caller believes it requested, which puts a wrong number in the record, while honouring the request is the unbounded read the ceiling exists to prevent
tail_bound_ceiling.measured: the bound is measured with a byte-counting handle in 7 independent cases, including one that goes through `_tail(..., permitted_root=...)`, the wrapper the lifecycle step actually calls; the contract guard pins the number of measurement points so deleting one fails the guard
tail_bound_ceiling.bytes_read_meaning: bytes_read remains the number of bytes the read returned, including the boundary probe byte, so it measures I/O rather than restating the cap; the published window is never larger than byte_limit

window_boundary_rule.rule: the single allowed probe byte is read from `start - 1` instead of past the end, and the first line is dropped only when that byte proves it is a fragment; a window that begins on a line boundary keeps its first line and reports dropped_partial_first_line=false
window_boundary_rule.why_the_front: a byte past the end cannot detect growth of more than one byte, and asking for more than one spare byte would break the ceiling; the front probe answers the question the published flag claims to answer, within the same budget
window_boundary_rule.growth: growth past the measured end is detected by re-seeking to the end of the same handle and publishing grew_during_read, and the newest bytes measured before the growth are preserved rather than clipped away
window_boundary_rule.fragment_label: a one-line window keeps its fragment and publishes first_line_is_fragment=true, because emptying the tail of a huge single-line log would hide the only evidence the failure left
window_boundary_rule.shrink: a file that shrinks below the window during the read is reported as unreadable with zero bytes, never as an empty or complete log

windows_gate_cause.what_fails: the Windows job fails in 'Windows database, import, auth and packaging regression suite', the 27-file pytest run, with 7 to 9 of its steps skipped as a consequence and the acceptance report step reporting that no release metadata exists to describe.
windows_gate_cause.reasoning: _Win32HandleMetadata.attach handed the verified handle to msvcrt.open_osfhandle with os.O_RDONLY only.  On Windows a CRT descriptor without _O_BINARY is opened in the default translation mode, so every CRLF in the object is folded to LF inside the read: the stream still looks like the log, but it is shorter than the size GetFileInformationByHandle measured on the same handle, the reported bytes_read is no longer the number of bytes the object holds, and a tail that starts mid-object starts at the wrong offset.  POSIX hosts have no text mode, so no Linux run -- CI or local -- can observe it.
windows_gate_cause.why_it_was_green_before: the assertions that compare a measured read against the object's byte count are new in M42.9; the files M42.8 asserted over were written with write_bytes or contain no CRLF, and translation only bites when CRLF is present, which is the normal shape of a Windows installer log.
windows_gate_cause.confidence: reasoned from the code, from the documented CRT behaviour, and from which assertions are Windows-sensitive; NOT confirmed by a run on a Windows host, which is what the next Windows job decides.  Stated as a cause with that limit on it rather than as a proven diagnosis.

the_silence_is_itself_a_defect.promise: the regression step states that 'every failing test is listed in the job summary and workflow annotations', and packaging/junit_report.py documents that a failing step 'always publishes an actionable ... annotation'.
the_silence_is_itself_a_defect.reality: the step failed and published neither.  The reason is structural: pytest writes the JUnit report only when it reaches the end of a run, so a run that is interrupted, aborted or refused leaves the parser with nothing to convert -- the parser's own stdout error is not an annotation, no summary file is written, and the check run shows only 'Process completed with exit code 1'.  A red step that says nothing is indistinguishable from a failure whose evidence was suppressed.
the_silence_is_itself_a_defect.second_finding: the build step of the same workflow already carries two guards for a related hazard -- $ErrorActionPreference relaxed around redirected native pipelines and $PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $false -- because pwsh 7.3+ treats a line on a native command's stderr as a terminating error under the runner's Stop preference.  The test step had no such guard, so any warning pytest prints on stderr could abort the step before the report existed.  That is a candidate mechanism for the observed no-report shape, not a proven cause: the log that would confirm it is behind a sign-in this sandbox does not have.

authenticode_root_cause_found_in_the_lau.why: every record since the first instrumented run has carried `cmdlet=missing` beside a refused `Microsoft.PowerShell.Security` import, and the earlier readings attributed that to the runner image being unable to answer.  The cause is not the image.  It is the launch environment this repository builds, and it is corrected here.

the_cause.observation_being_explained: `security_module_import=failed` with the host's own message `The following error occurred while loading the extended type data file: Error in TypeData "System.Security.AccessControl.ObjectSecurity": The member A... is already present`, and `cmdlet=missing` reported separately beside it, on Windows PowerShell 5.1.20348.5622, with both executables `UNKNOWN`
the_cause.mechanism: every step of the Windows workflow runs under `shell: pwsh`, which is PowerShell 7, so the Python process inherits a `PSModulePath` whose entries name PowerShell 7's module directories ahead of the ones Windows PowerShell ships with.  `run_powershell` passed `dict(os.environ)` to the child unchanged, so those directories reached `powershell.exe` -- Windows PowerShell 5.1 -- and its `Import-Module Microsoft.PowerShell.Security` resolved the PowerShell 7 copy of the module (7.0.0.0 from the PowerShell 7 module directory) instead of its own (3.0.0.0 from `WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules`).  Since PowerShell 7.3 that manifest carries `TypesToProcess = "Security.types.ps1xml"`, whose `System.Security.AccessControl.ObjectSecurity` type data adds members the .NET Framework already provides on 5.1, so the import aborts with a format-XML update failure, the module never loads, and every cmdlet it owns -- `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` among them -- becomes unresolvable
the_cause.why_this_is_not_inference_from_the_wordi: the mechanism is the documented behaviour of this exact failure and the remediation is the one the PowerShell team recommends for it (unset `PSModulePath` for the `powershell.exe` child so Windows PowerShell rebuilds its own default from the registry).  The repository is the responsible party, which is checkable in this tree: the workflow's steps declare `shell: pwsh`, and `run_powershell` copied the parent environment verbatim
the_cause.what_would_confirm_it: a Windows run whose `security_module_import` is the import outcome and whose per-file rows are determinate.  Until that run exists, the diagnosis is the strongest supported one and not a confirmed observation, and every existing `UNKNOWN` stays correct for the environment it was produced in
the_cause.what_it_does_not_establish: it says nothing about whether the release is signed.  No signing identity exists in this repository by design; owner decision A is unchanged and untouched by this correction

the_correction.what_it_does: returns a copy of the parent environment with `PSModulePath` removed -- the comparison is case-insensitive, because Windows environment names are, so a differently-cased parent cannot smuggle one spelling past a case-sensitive filter -- and reports whether anything was removed
the_correction.where_it_is_applied: `run_powershell`, the only place in this repository that starts `powershell.exe`; the caller's other environment settings are left untouched, and the queried path still travels out of band in `DRILLMASTER_TARGET_PATH` rather than being interpolated into the script
